column2: On November first, a business jet fell more than six miles out of the sky in a little over a minute.

It was a Learjet sixty, a charter flight carrying seven passengers and two pilots from Austin to the Bahamas. It cruised at forty-one thousand feet, then descended to around thirty-five thousand as it crossed Florida.
But South Florida was full of thunderstorms that afternoon. The crew reported light clear ice and moderate turbulence, and asked to climb. Controllers cleared them to thirty-seven thousand feet.
Seconds later, a mayday. The crew reported descending ten thousand feet per minute. Then an overspeed at twenty thousand. Then twenty-two thousand feet per minute, in a sixty-degree bank.
The jet hit the ground nose-down on a busy road in Palm Beach County. All nine people on board were killed. Remarkably, only one person on the ground was reported hurt.

So how does a jet fall like that? At high altitude, the gap between flying too slow and too fast gets very narrow, and ice and turbulence can push a plane toward either edge. Investigators are also looking at something else: evidence that part of the left elevator, the surface that pitches the nose up and down, may have separated before impact.
The N.T.S.B. has recovered the cockpit voice recorder. Its preliminary report should come in a few weeks, but the full answer to why this jet fell will likely take a year or more.
